Trailer Review 

I bought the BOB one-wheel trailer to experience  trailer touring.  Many bikers have recommended the BOB over all others.  It was very cheap find, 100 usd for a 300 usd + value if new.

Now I understand the pros and cons of trailer touring at a personal level, and now know that I prefer a good set of dry-bag roll-up panniers for my touring style.

The one-wheel trailer trails behind the bike perfectly, and is stable even when fully-loaded at high speeds downhill. The bike handles and corners beautifully.  It's easier for accessing gear and setting up camp once a campsite is found and established. 

It's simple, being a single-track unit with only one-wheel, and a very effective axle hitch system. It's much nicer to pull than a two wheel trailer, but a two wheel trailer would carry more weight. 

For my touring and camping style, I prefer dry-sack roll-up rear panniers. I've learned to travel very light, and although plenty of cargo space is nice to have, I don't require so much.

One issue is that a rider cannot backup or make a short radius turn-around.  Getting in and out of tight spaces is not an option. 

For my purposes, this is especially important when stealth camping, cutting into dense forests to find a suitable campsite, getting up and down a small set of steps of an abandoned structure, or when exploring situations where pulling a trailer is just not a good option. 

The BOB trailer is a good option for local hauling or defined day trips, but not suitable for minimalistic stealth camping, especially off-road exploring. 

I prefer panniers, where I can actually lift my bike while standing over it, and spin it around 180 degrees. Panniers are also preferable anytime when negotiating steps or cutting into dense forested areas.  

In all situations, panniers offer more stealth.

The BOB trailer recently tested.

https://www.amazon.com/gp/aw/d/B000RH7GKS

The two-wheeler trailer attached to my Peugeot touring bike. I fabricated and tested this trailer last year for local hauling and left both the trailer and bike behind, back in my hometown.

The two-wheel trailer holds a larger and heavier load, but is not as stable as the one-wheeler.

Two wheels on a trailer leaves behind three tracks, whereas an in-line single wheel trailer leaves behind a single track.
